title: Pep Guardiola and a strange sideshow that led to a two-match ban (but not the Carabao Cup final)
content:
At the final whistle, Pep Guardiola made a beeline for the three men in the centre circle who seemed to be doing their best to avoid eye contact with Manchester City’s manager.

In particular, he wanted to shake hands with the referee, Sam Barrott, flanked either side by his two assistants. Yet here’s the thing: not every handshake is a sign of friendliness. Sometimes, indeed, it can be a show of hostility dressed up as cordiality. And this, from Guardiola, was undoubtedly one of those occasions.

He was riled, to say the least, by Barrott’s refereeing during City’s freewheeling 3-1 win over Newcastle United and what was — ignoring, for one moment, the depth of Guardiola’s rage — a satisfying night for the team trying to make history by reaching four FA Cup finals in a row.

We can also be sure that it wasn’t just Barrott’s decision not to award a foul against Kieran Trippier that was eating away at City’s manager. No, this was an accumulation of stored-up grievances against the refereeing industry as a whole.

When Guardiola talked afterwards about City having “all the records in this country, for the referees”, it was the kind of sentence that would usually be more associated with Sir Alex Ferguson or Jose Mourinho. He then mentioned, as if joking, that he was now the proud recipient of one of those records. Again, though, you would have to be naive to think he was genuinely celebrating.

“We have the manager with the record for the most yellow cards… I’m so proud of that,” he said, heavy with sarcasm. “I always wanted a new record, and now I have it. Two games banned now (for me), so I will go on holiday and the team will continue.”

That, at least, was half right. Nobody should imagine he will go on holiday, but his sixth yellow card of the season means a two-match touchline ban, taking in City’s game away at West Ham United in the Premier League next weekend and, almost certainly, a to-be-arranged FA Cup quarter-final (he is exempt from the Carabao Cup final against Arsenal because the competition has its own disciplinary rules).

Speaking on TNT Sports, Guardiola was invited to disclose what he had been shouting at Barrott, over and again, in the moments after Omar Marmoush’s second goal made it 3-1 to the away side.

Guardiola’s explanation was laced with sarcasm: “I’m sorry! I’m sorry! I’m sorry!”

Sorry for what? “For how good we were playing.”

To which, the follow-up question really should have been: why would you think this referee, or any referee, wanted you to play badly?

If Guardiola had not looked so utterly delighted during other moments of his pitch-walk, you might have thought that the stresses and strains of the last week — falling seven points behind Arsenal at the top of the Premier League — were affecting him.

In fact, some observers thought he risked a red card for his aggressive reaction to the fourth official, Lewis Smith, squaring up to him and clenching his fist. It is quite possible the Football Association will review all the footage and decide that, yes, he crossed the line about what is acceptable and what is not.

Yet Guardiola has not made his reputation as one of the greatest coaches in history by succumbing to end-of-season pressure. And, besides, he could be seen bear-hugging his players, as well as those of Newcastle, within moments of being led away from Barrott, twice turning back to shout and angrily gesticulate in the referee’s direction. That was the strangest thing of all: how quickly he lurched from rage to joviality and then back again, like turning a tap on and off.

As the match officials made their way off the pitch, Guardiola was planting a kiss on the cheek of his goalkeeper, James Trafford, and waving, almost dewy-eyed, towards the City fans in the most vertiginous parts of St James’ Park.

It was a strange sideshow — the different faces of Guardiola, all in one night — and the thought did occur that a man with his experience and, yes, greatness should not really have made himself the story this way.

Yes, nobody wants blandness from managers. Surely, though, he ought to have realised he was going to incur a yellow card for his response to Trippier getting away with a foul on Jeremy Doku? Did he have to lose the plot that way, throwing his arms around like a man fighting off an invisible swarm of wasps? Was it really worth the ban that, by his own admission, he knew was inevitable?

Guardiola has served a one-match ban, from the FA Cup tie at home to Exeter City, for collecting three yellow cards, so that will be three games in total when he has not been permitted in the dugout.

Or to put it another way, what would he say if one of his players did the same and ended up with a suspension at this stage of the season? That it was needless, unprofessional and entirely avoidable, presumably.

When the dust settles, perhaps Guardiola may reflect that, regardless of whether Barrott is a good, bad or appalling referee, there were valid reasons why the FA felt it necessary to try to find a way of improving manager behaviour in the technical area. Or maybe, on reflection, he won’t. The impression he gave on Saturday was that he didn’t care less about that side of things.

It was similar at the same stadium two months ago after City won in the Carabao Cup, when Guardiola went on a lengthy rant about VAR after his team had a goal ruled out for offside.

This weekend, Guardiola spoke with the air of a man who had been the victim of one-sided refereeing so many times that he felt duty-bound to speak up, and to hell with the consequences. “I will not shut up,” was another line. “I will not be silent. Many, many, many, many times, this has happened.”

Why, he asked, had Trippier not been penalised for pulling back Doku, in full flight, eight minutes into the second half?

“Listen, when Jeremy Doku dribbles (past) Trippier, and goes all the way to the box, and he’s pulled from behind, I’m not asking for a yellow card. But please, it’s a foul. Or maybe, except in this country, it’s a foul.”

After a brief pause, Guardiola continued unprompted: “Oh my God. Oh my God. There are things after 10 years (in England) I cannot understand. Review the action. Of course I’m going to defend Doku and all my teams.”

It was quite some outburst from a manager who, a minute earlier, had described City’s win as their best performance at St James’ Park during his decade at the club. He did, in fairness, mention Savinho’s wing-play, the goals of Marmoush and how satisfying it was to reach the quarter-finals eight seasons on the bounce.

Yet Guardiola, like most managers, tends to see only the decisions that go against his team, and not the ones that go in their favour. It’s a common trait of his profession and, on a night when there was so much to enjoy about City’s performance, perhaps he should just have restricted himself, on reflection, to praise of his players.
